title: What a proposal should contain
metaTitle: What a design proposal should contain
excerpt: A useful proposal names the pages or the product slice, what is out of scope, what you will own, and how you will talk. A mood board is not a proposal.
alt: A person in a blue shirt signing a paper document with a pen, the moment a scope becomes a record for an article about what a proposal must contain.
caption: A document, a pen, and a decision being recorded. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a design proposal include?
faqs.answer: Name the pages or the product slice, the states that count as done, what is out of scope, what the client will own at the end, and how you will communicate. Include who decides and what you need from them. A proposal that only describes a feeling cannot be accepted, because nobody can tell when it has been delivered.

faqs.question: Should a proposal include a price?
faqs.answer: Yes, with the role attached. Say what the price covers and what would change it, such as a new audience or a new set of screens. A range is honest when the slice is still soft, if you also say what will firm the number. A number with no boundary is a guess both sides will argue about later.

faqs.question: How long should the document be?
faqs.answer: Long enough to name the work and the exclusions, short enough that a founder will read it. A few pages beat a deck that repeats the same ambition. If a section does not help someone decide or deliver, cut it. Process diagrams that could describe any studio are the usual cut.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
A design proposal structure is a list of decisions a founder can accept. Name the pages or the product slice. Name what is out of scope. Name what the client will own. Name how you will talk. A mood is not a proposal. A mood cannot be delivered, so it cannot be finished, so it cannot be paid for without a fight.

Write it for the person who was not on the call. They will read it later and decide whether the invoice matches the promise. If that person would be confused, the document is not done.

## The slice of work, in nouns

Start with the thing that will exist. For a site: the pages, and the job of each. Home, the offer, proof, a way to start a conversation. For a product: the workflow, and the states. Empty, error, success, and the one path a new user finishes. Nouns beat adjectives. "A premium digital experience" is not a slice. "These four pages, in English, on a phone and a desktop" is.

Say what "done" means for each piece. A page is done when the offer is understandable, the action works, and the content is the client's real content, not lorem. A screen is done when the path can be completed with the empty and error states written. If you leave done implied, you will relitigate it in the last week, when everyone is tired.

Attach the assumptions. You have the logo, or you do not. You will write the first draft of the sentences, or the client will. There is one language. There is one audience. Assumptions that stay verbal become surprises. Surprises become scope. Write them under the list, in short lines a person can correct before they sign.

[Google's guidance on title links](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) is a reminder that a title should describe the page. Use that habit on the proposal's own title. "Proposal for the marketing site, four pages" tells the reader what they are holding. "Partnership journey" does not. The document can still be warm. It has to be findable in a folder six months later.

## Out of scope, in the same voice

The exclusions are not an insult. They are how the date survives. Name the neighboring work you will not do in this slice. A brand system beyond a small type and color pass. A native app. A migration of five years of blog posts. Copy for a second audience. Illustration in a style you have not shown. Each exclusion prevents a reasonable person from assuming it was included.

Write exclusions as plainly as the inclusions. A joking "we will not boil the ocean" does not help. "We will not redesign the product application in this project" does. If a piece might be next, say it is next, not now. The founder can still want it. They can see that wanting it is a second decision.

[People-first content guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks whether a reader can tell the purpose of a page. A proposal has a purpose: a yes or a no on a defined slice. Sections that exist to perform taste, with no bearing on the slice, dilute that purpose. One relevant project is enough proof. A tour of the studio's philosophy can live on the site, where it belongs.

If you are a partner rather than a vendor, say that the slice may change when you learn, and say how a change is agreed. "A new page requires a written add." That sentence is kinder than a fight. If you are executing a spec, say that the spec attached is the slice, and that new screens are a change. The role and the exclusions have to agree. A partner proposal with vendor exclusions, or the reverse, is the unnamed relationship again.

## Ownership, access, and the files

Say what the client will hold at the end. The repository. The domain. The hosting account. The content logins. The brand files. If any of these stay with the studio, say so, and say what happens if the engagement ends. "You own the site" is incomplete if the fonts are unlicensed or the photos cannot be used on the web. List the licenses you will buy, and who they are assigned to.

Name the place notes will live during the work. On a Hanabi project that place includes the client portal: brand files, docs, and updates after delivery, so the decision is not only in a chat. Whatever the tool, write it down. A proposal that skips this leaves the handoff as a scramble, and the scramble is where the second project goes to die.

Say what you need from them, and when. Content by a date. Access to the current site. One decision-maker. Feedback within a set number of days. These are not demands for their own sake. They are the other half of the date. A timeline that ignores them is fiction. Put their obligations next to yours, so the schedule is a shared object.

Mention the stack when it affects ownership. A marketing site in Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind, deployed on Vercel, is a concrete thing they can keep. A prototype that lives only in a tool they do not have a seat for is a different promise. Say which one this price buys. Figma files, if you design there, should be in an account they can access, not only in yours.

## How you will talk

Name the rhythm. A weekly review. A shared staging link they can open without you. Notes after the review, with the decision in a sentence. One channel for requests, so work does not arrive from three inboxes and contradict itself. Same-day replies can be a standard for questions. They should not be a promise to redesign overnight. Say the difference.

Name who is in the work. The people the founder met, or a team the founder has not met. A small studio's advantage is that design and build sit together. If that is true, say it. If production will involve someone new, say that too. A proposal that implies a relationship the calendar will not keep is the start of the disappointment.

Say how feedback should look. Comments on the staging page or in the design file, tied to the job of the screen. "This fails the offer" is usable. "Make it more premium" needs a translation, and the proposal can say you will ask for the translation. You are teaching the working method before the project, which is part of what they are buying.

Include a simple change rule. Small copy edits inside the slice are included, up to a review or two. A new audience, a new product area, or a new set of pages is a change, written down, with an effect on the date. Founders accept this when it is visible at the start. They resent it when it appears as a defense.

## Price, date, and the risks you can see

Put the price next to the slice, not in a fog of options. If there are two options, they should be two slices, not two moods at two prices. Say what is included: design, build, a launch window, a short period of fixes after launch. Say what would change the price. Another language. A rush. Content you expected and did not receive, if that will stall the team.

Give a date that depends on the assumptions. "Four weeks from the day we have the content and the kickoff, assuming feedback within three business days." A date with no assumptions is a wish. A range is acceptable when discovery is part of the slice, if the proposal says what ends the range. "We will confirm the date after the sitemap is agreed, in week one."

Name risks you already see. The current site's content is scattered. The brand has three logos. The product workflow is not settled. A risk named in the proposal is a sign you were listening. A proposal that pretends the path is smooth, when the call was full of knots, will not be trusted by the careful reader. You do not need to solve the knots in the document. You need to show you saw them.

Skip the fake precision. Hours estimated to the half hour, for work that includes judgment, look serious and are usually decorative. A slice, a price, and a date with assumptions are more honest. If you track time internally, that can stay internal. The founder needs to know what they will have, what they will pay, and what they must do.

## What to leave out of the document

Leave out the stock process that could be any studio's. Discover, define, design, deliver, with four icons. If your weeks are specific, two sentences on how a review works will do more. A generic diagram is a tell that the slice is also generic.

Leave out claims you cannot stand next to. Guaranteed rankings. A transformation in thirty days. A quote from a client you would not ask to repeat. Invented timelines from past work. The proposal will be reread. Write only what you want reread.

Leave out a second sales pitch. They are already in the document. One proof point, tied to a similar constraint, is enough. Down the Cove for a commerce move. Thomas Bewick for an editorial heritage site. Got Next or Leadly for a product interface. Pick the neighbor of this project. A gallery turns the proposal back into a website.

Keep the file easy to read. Short headings. Real pages named. A founder should be able to accept it from a phone between meetings. If they cannot find the slice, the exclusions, the ownership, and the price in one pass, edit until they can.

The proposal is also the seed of the second project, if you want one. A handoff that is only a zip file, with the people who knew the decisions gone, is how the next engagement dies. [How agencies lose the second project](/blog/how-agencies-lose-the-second-project) is about leaving a system and a way back to the same team. Read it before you write a final invoice that is also a goodbye you did not intend.

When the slice is clear enough to put in a document, book [an intro call with Hanabi](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring what you think the pages are, and what you hope is included. The call should end with a smaller, truer list, which is the beginning of a proposal worth signing.
